decisions.quote:
We extended this line of research to consider whether pronunciation errors
in Mandarin Chinese are processed differently when a foreign-accented speaker makes
them relative to when a native-accented speaker makes them (a conceptual replication
using the materials from Pelzl et al., 2019).
decisions.reason: Both the shipped record and blind coding agree on type='replication'. The paper collects new behavioral and ERP data from a new sample of native Mandarin listeners to re-test tone and rhyme mismatch effects using the design and stimuli of Pelzl et al. (2019).

in Mandarin Chinese are processed differently when a foreign-accented speaker makes
them relative to when a native-accented speaker makes them (a conceptual replication
using the materials from Pelzl et al., 2019).
decisions.reason: Wrong original in shipped row: the shipped record lists Pelzl et al. (2020; 10.1017/s1366728920000280), which is only cited in passing as background on down-weighting (lines 286, 1038). The paper explicitly states that it is a conceptual replication using the design and materials of Pelzl et al. (2019; 10.1017/S0272263117000444) and directly compares its behavioral and ERP results against Pelzl et al. (2019). Thus row 261 pairs with blind target 0.

decisions.quote:
First, our results are consistent with behavioral outcomes from Pelzl et al.
(2019), who found less accuracy for tone mismatches relative to rhymes both
in a disyllabic lexical decision task and in a sentence judgment task that used
a subset of the stimuli used here (with only the native Mandarin speaker).
However, consistent with other ERP studies reviewed above (Brown-Schmidt
& Canseco-Gonzalez, 2004; Schirmer et al., 2005), Pelzl et al. (2019) failed
to find statistically significant ERP differences between tone and rhyme mis-
matches, unlike the current study.
decisions.reason: With original identity resolved to Pelzl et al. (2019), both shipped and blind coding agree on outcome='mixed'. The authors report that their behavioral results (lower accuracy for tone than rhyme mismatches) and word/nonword N400 duration trends replicated Pelzl et al. (2019), whereas their ERP comparison between tone and rhyme mismatches differed from Pelzl et al. (2019).
